name: Silk Roads
other_names: Silk Road; Seidenstraße; overland Silk Routes
date_note: conventional start with Han envoy Zhang Qian's missions c.138–126 BCE; steppe exchange far older; decline after c.1450 debated
making_significance: Relay routes across Eurasia carried silk, paper-making, glass, metalwork, textile patterns, pigments and travelling craftspeople between China, Central Asia, Iran, South Asia and the Mediterranean.
object_types: silk textiles; glass vessels; silver vessels; paper; ceramics; manuscripts
defined_by: Ferdinand von Richthofen (term Seidenstraße, 1877); historians; UNESCO (Chang'an–Tianshan corridor, 2014)
leaves_out: The name privileges silk and the two ends; it leaves out steppe herders, oasis makers, non-silk goods, and the relay character of most exchange.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); International Dunhuang Programme (link out); Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Staatliche Museen zu Berlin SMB-digital (CC BY-SA where marked)
notes: Umbrella node: members include steppe route, oasis route, Tea Horse Road and Sogdian diaspora.

name: Steppe route
date_note: east–west movement of horses, chariots and metallurgy from the 3rd–2nd millennium BCE; Mongol-era (13th–14th c.) peak; ongoing in altered form
making_significance: Mobile pastoralists moved horse gear, chariot technology, bronze metallurgy, felt and gold animal-style ornament across the grasslands from Hungary to Mongolia.
materials_techniques: felt making; bronze casting; gold working; horse tack
object_types: felt; gold plaques; bronze knives; chariots; saddles
leaves_out: Framing as 'route' can hide that herders were makers and patrons, not only carriers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports; Europeana
notes: Much evidence is from kurgan burials (funerary sensitivity).

name: Oasis route (Tarim Basin)
other_names: northern and southern Silk Roads around the Taklamakan
date_note: Han to late first millennium CE; approximate
making_significance: Oasis cities such as Dunhuang, Turfan, Kucha, Khotan and Kashgar were workshops and relay points for silk, jade, wall painting, manuscripts and Buddhist image-making.
materials_techniques: wall painting; silk weaving; jade working; manuscript copying
functions: exchange and value;record and writing;ritual and belief
leaves_out: The early-20th-c. removals of Dunhuang and Turfan material to European and Japanese collections are part of this history.
free_sources: International Dunhuang Programme (link out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Staatliche Museen zu Berlin SMB-digital (CC BY-SA where marked)
notes: Dunhuang Library Cave removals (1907–) relevant to F1.24.

name: Tea Horse Road
other_names: Chamadao; Ancient Tea Horse Road; Southern Silk Road (partly)
date_note: Song-dynasty tea-for-horses trade formalised 11th c.; Tang origins claimed; porterage into the 20th c.
making_significance: Mule caravans and human porters carried compressed brick tea from Yunnan and Sichuan to Tibet in exchange for horses, wool and medicinal goods.
leaves_out: Porters' labour (many carried loads over 100 kg) is rarely centred.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles
notes: Term 'Chamagudao' dates from 1990s scholarship.

name: Indian Ocean world
other_names: Indian Ocean trade; Maritime Silk Road (western)
date_note: from Harappan–Gulf contact c.2500 BCE; monsoon sailing documented by 1st c. CE; ongoing
making_significance: Monsoon-timed sailing linked textile, bead, ceramic and metal makers from East Africa to China, spreading cotton cloth, glass beads, stoneware and shipbuilding know-how.
materials_techniques: monsoon sailing; sewn-plank boats; cotton weaving; bead making
object_types: beads; cotton textiles; stoneware jars; porcelain; ivory
defined_by: historians (e.g. K.N. Chaudhuri; Abdul Sheriff); archaeologists
leaves_out: Enslaved people moved through the same circuits; coastal and island makers are often reduced to entrepôts.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); British Museum EMKP (CC); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports
notes: Umbrella node; sub-circuits Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, South China Sea.

name: Arabian Sea circuit
date_note: Harappan–Gulf phase c.2500 BCE; Periplus of the Erythraean Sea 1st c. CE; ongoing
making_significance: The western Indian Ocean circuit moved Gujarati and Malabar textiles, pepper, beads, incense and Chinese ceramics between India, Arabia, the Red Sea and East Africa.
materials_techniques: dhow building; cotton weaving; bead making
defined_by: historians; the Periplus (1st c. CE Greek text)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Internet Archive (public-domain texts); open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Bay of Bengal circuit
date_note: Khao Sam Kaeo and Arikamedu evidence from 4th–1st c. BCE; ongoing
making_significance: Exchange between eastern India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia carried glass and stone beads, rouletted ware, Buddhist and Hindu image-making and textile patterns.
materials_techniques: drawn glass beads; stone bead drilling; cotton painting
object_types: Indo-Pacific beads; rouletted ware; bronze images; textiles
leaves_out: South Asian craftspeople working in Southeast Asian ports.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: South China Sea circuit
date_note: first millennium BCE (jade, bronze drums); intensive from 9th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Exchange between southern China, Vietnam, the Philippines and the Malay world carried jade, bronze drums, stoneware, porcelain, forest products and shipbuilding traditions.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports
notes: Overlaps Maritime Jade Road and Nanhai route.

name: Nanhai route
other_names: South Sea route; Maritime Silk Road (Chinese side)
date_note: Han references; Song–Yuan peak at Guangzhou and Quanzhou
making_significance: Chinese ports shipped stoneware, porcelain, silk and iron to the south and west; wrecks such as Belitung (c.830) and Nanhai One (12th c.) preserve whole cargoes.
materials_techniques: kiln mass production; packing in storage jars
object_types: Changsha bowls; celadon; iron bars; silk
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); open-access journal articles
notes: Belitung cargo recovery (commercial salvage) raised ethical debate — check framing.

name: Trans-Saharan trade
date_note: camel caravans from c.3rd–4th c. CE; earlier Garamantian links; decline late 19th c.
making_significance: Camel caravans exchanged West African gold, salt, copper, glass, textiles and books, and carried Maghribi and Sahelian styles of building, leatherwork and manuscript making.
materials_techniques: leatherwork; copper alloy casting; manuscript copying; salt cutting
object_types: gold; salt slabs; Tuareg leatherwork; manuscripts; beads
leaves_out: Enslaved people were moved across the Sahara; Tuareg and Sahelian makers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; British Museum EMKP (CC); open-access excavation reports
notes: Timbuktu manuscripts: some digitised open (check licences).

name: Kilwa gold route
other_names: Sofala gold trade; Zimbabwe Plateau–Kilwa trade
date_note: Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe periods; approximate
making_significance: Gold from the Zimbabwe Plateau passed through Sofala to Kilwa, financing coral-stone building and coinage and bringing Chinese porcelain and Indian beads inland.
materials_techniques: gold mining; coral-stone masonry; coin striking
object_types: gold; Kilwa coins; glass beads; porcelain sherds
leaves_out: Local miners and Shona-speaking makers are often subordinated to coastal narratives.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); open-access excavation reports

name: Swahili dhow trade
other_names: monsoon dhow trade; mtepe and jahazi trade
date_note: from c.8th c.; ongoing on a small scale (Lamu, Zanzibar)
making_significance: Monsoon dhows moved mangrove poles, ivory, textiles, carved doors and ceramics between the East African coast, Arabia and India, and carried boat-building skills.
materials_techniques: sewn and nailed plank boats; coral-stone building; wood carving
object_types: dhows; carved doors; textiles; mangrove poles
leaves_out: 19th-c. trafficking of enslaved people through Zanzibar.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); open-access excavation reports

name: Cowrie shell currency network
date_note: cowries in Shang China c.1200 BCE; Maldivian cowries to Bengal and West Africa to 19th c.
making_significance: Maldivian Monetaria moneta shells served as money from Bengal to West Africa, shipped as ballast by European companies and used to buy enslaved people.
functions: exchange and value;clothing and adornment;ritual and belief
defined_by: historians (Hogendorn and Johnson, 'The Shell Money of the Slave Trade', 1986)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); British Museum EMKP (CC); Wikimedia Commons

name: Ivory trade
date_note: multiple eras; ancient Egyptian and Aegean trade; 19th-c. caravan trade most documented; CITES ban 1989
making_significance: Elephant ivory moved from Africa and South Asia to carvers in China, India, Europe and the Mediterranean; 19th-c. demand for piano keys and billiard balls drove caravan trade.
functions: exchange and value;rule and display;play and music
leaves_out: Enslaved porters carried tusks in 19th-c. East and Central Africa; looted Benin ivories (1897).
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Walters Art Museum (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: European glass trade-bead circulation
date_note: Venetian, Bohemian and Dutch beads exported from late 15th c.
making_significance: Venetian, Bohemian and Dutch glass beads were exchanged in Africa and the Americas, where makers reworked them into regalia and beadwork.
object_types: chevron beads; seed beads; beaded regalia
leaves_out: Beads were among goods exchanged for enslaved Africans.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Wikimedia Commons

name: Dilmun–Magan–Meluhha trade
date_note: Akkadian texts name Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (Indus region)
making_significance: Maritime trade brought Magan copper, Indus carnelian beads and seals, and timber to Mesopotamia, recorded in cuneiform and seen in Ur's royal tombs.
materials_techniques: copper smelting; carnelian bead drilling; seal carving
object_types: etched carnelian beads; Gulf seals; copper ingots
leaves_out: Identification of Meluhha with the Indus region is a scholarly consensus, not a self-name.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link out); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Old Assyrian trade (Aššur–Kaneš)
other_names: Kültepe trade; Old Assyrian merchant colonies
date_note: Kültepe (Kaneš) level II and Ib
making_significance: Assyrian merchant families shipped tin and textiles by donkey caravan to Anatolia for silver and gold, documented in some 23,000 cuneiform letters.
materials_techniques: donkey caravans; textile weaving (women in Aššur); tin trade
leaves_out: Assyrian women who wove textiles for export and wrote letters.
free_sources: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (link out); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lapis lazuli route
date_note: lapis in Mehrgarh earlier; Mesopotamian and Egyptian use from 4th millennium BCE
making_significance: Lapis lazuli from Sar-i Sang in Badakhshan reached Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Indus, where it was carved into beads, inlays and seals.
functions: exchange and value;clothing and adornment;rule and display
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
notes: Ur royal cemetery material is funerary.

name: Anatolian obsidian network
date_note: Epipalaeolithic to Chalcolithic; approximate
making_significance: Obsidian from Göllü Dağ and Nenezi Dağ in Cappadocia travelled to the Levant and Cyprus as blades, cores and mirrors (Çatalhöyük).
materials_techniques: pressure blade making; grinding and polishing
defined_by: archaeologists (obsidian sourcing, Renfrew, Dixon and Cann 1960s)
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons; Open Context (CC BY)
notes: Aegean Melos obsidian (Franchthi, c.11th millennium BCE) is a parallel network.

name: Late Bronze Age Eastern Mediterranean exchange
date_note: 'Bronze Age' as defined for the Aegean and Near East
making_significance: Palace and merchant trade moved copper oxhide ingots, tin, glass ingots, ebony, ivory and textiles between Egypt, Cyprus, the Levant, Anatolia and the Aegean, as shown by the Uluburun wreck.
materials_techniques: oxhide ingot casting; glass ingot making
leaves_out: Nubian gold and ebony producers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Phoenician network
date_note: Iron Age; to fall of Carthage 146 BCE
making_significance: Phoenician cities and colonies carried purple-dyed cloth, carved ivory, metal bowls, glass and the alphabet across the Mediterranean to Iberia and North Africa.
materials_techniques: purple dyeing; ivory carving; core-formed glass; metal chasing
object_types: ivories; metal bowls; glass; purple cloth
leaves_out: 'Phoenician' is a Greek name; the people called themselves by city (e.g. Tyrians).
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports; Europeana

name: Roman Mediterranean trade
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Roman shipping standardised amphorae, terra sigillata, marble, glass and grain across the Mediterranean and linked it to the Red Sea and India.
materials_techniques: terra sigillata moulding; glassblowing; marble quarrying
leaves_out: Enslaved workers produced and moved much of this trade.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Europeana; open-access excavation reports

name: Medieval Mediterranean trade
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Islamic, Byzantine and Italian traders moved silks, lustreware, paper, glass, alum and sugar between the Levant, Egypt, the Maghrib, Iberia and Italy.
defined_by: historians (e.g. S.D. Goitein; Olivia Remie Constable)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Cambridge Digital Library Taylor-Schechter Genizah (link out)

name: Venetian and Genoese trade networks
date_note: Byzantine privileges for Venice 1082; Venice falls 1797; Genoese colonies to 15th–16th c.
making_significance: Venetian and Genoese colonies from Crete to Caffa moved silks, alum, spices and glass, and supported Murano glass and Italian silk weaving.
leaves_out: Genoese trafficking of enslaved people via Caffa and Black Sea ports.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Wikimedia Commons; Europeana

name: Amber Road
date_note: Baltic amber in Mycenaean graves from c.1600 BCE; Roman Aquileia trade
making_significance: Baltic amber moved south to Mycenaean Greece, Etruria and Roman Aquileia, where it was carved into beads, pendants and figures.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; Europeana

name: Bronze Age tin routes
date_note: approximate; sources and routes debated
making_significance: Tin, needed for tin bronze, travelled long distances from sources such as Cornwall, the Erzgebirge, Iberia and Central Asia.
leaves_out: Sources of Near Eastern tin remain debated.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons
notes: Check current isotope-provenance literature.

name: Varangian route
other_names: route from the Varangians to the Greeks
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Scandinavian traders moved along the Dnieper to Constantinople, exchanging furs, wax and enslaved people for silk, silver and glass.
leaves_out: Slavic, Finnic and Baltic peoples along the rivers.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Europeana; open-access excavation reports

name: Volga trade route
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Islamic silver dirhams flowed north via the Volga for furs, wax and enslaved people, filling Scandinavian and Baltic hoards.
leaves_out: Volga Bulgars and Khazars as intermediaries.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Europeana; open-access excavation reports

name: Hanseatic League
date_note: Lübeck refounded 1159; last Hanseatic diet 1669
making_significance: A league of merchant towns ran kontore in Bergen, London, Bruges and Novgorod, moving stockfish, furs, wax, cloth and amber in cog ships.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Europeana

name: Grand Trunk Road
date_note: Mauryan route; rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri 1540s; ongoing
making_significance: A trunk road from Bengal to Kabul carried goods, armies and craftspeople and was punctuated by serais, kos minars and wells.
defined_by: historians; the Mughal and British states
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Incense routes
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Caravans carried frankincense and myrrh from South Arabia and the Horn to the Mediterranean, funding Nabataean building at Petra and in the Negev.
defined_by: historians; UNESCO (Incense Route – Desert Cities in the Negev, 2005)
leaves_out: Harvesters in Dhofar and Somaliland.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out)

name: Red Sea network
date_note: Egyptian harbour at Wadi al-Jarf c.2600 BCE; Punt voyages; Berenike and Aksum; ongoing
making_significance: Red Sea harbours linked Egypt, Aksum and Arabia to the Indian Ocean, carrying incense, ivory, glass, textiles and pepper.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Cape Route and the East India companies
other_names: Carreira da Índia; VOC; English East India Company
date_note: da Gama 1498; VOC 1602–1799; English EIC to 1874
making_significance: Chartered companies shipped Asian textiles, porcelain, lacquer and spices to Europe and commissioned designs for European taste.
leaves_out: Company slave trading (e.g. VOC to the Cape) and colonial coercion.
free_sources: Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; British Library (public-domain digitised items)

name: Atlantic world trade
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Atlantic shipping moved plants, animals, metals, dyes and manufactured goods between Europe, Africa and the Americas, reshaping materials available to makers on all three continents.
materials_techniques: silver mining; dye production; plantation processing
leaves_out: Indigenous dispossession and forced labour; enslaved Africans (see separate node).
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Library of Congress (public-domain items); NYPL Digital Collections (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons; Rijksmuseum (public-domain images)

name: Transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans
other_names: transatlantic slave trade; triangular trade; Middle Passage
date_note: first direct Africa–Americas voyage c.1525; last documented voyage 1866–67
making_significance: About 12.5 million African people were forcibly embarked; their knowledge of rice cultivation, indigo, ironworking, textiles, building and music shaped making across the Americas.
materials_techniques: rice cultivation; indigo processing; ironwork; basketry
leaves_out: People are shown as people, never as goods; content note required.
free_sources: SlaveVoyages database (free; link out); Enslaved.org (free; link out); Library of Congress (public-domain items); NYPL Digital Collections (public-domain items)
notes: Show as movement of people with content note; figures from SlaveVoyages estimates.

name: Manila galleon trade
date_note: first return voyage 1565; last galleon 1815
making_significance: Galleons carried Mexican and Peruvian silver to Manila and Chinese silk, porcelain, lacquer and ivory to Acapulco, prompting enconchado painting, Puebla talavera and biombos.
leaves_out: Enslaved and indentured Asians ('chinos') carried to New Spain.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); LACMA (public-domain images); Wikimedia Commons; Rijksmuseum (public-domain images)

name: Mesoamerican obsidian network
date_note: Formative to Spanish conquest; approximate
making_significance: Obsidian from sources such as Pachuca, El Chayal and Ixtepeque moved as cores and prismatic blades, supporting workshops at Teotihuacan and across the Maya region.
materials_techniques: prismatic blade pressure technique; source quarrying
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Olmec horizon
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Shared motifs, jade and greenstone carving, iron-ore mirrors and ceramic styles spread among Formative Mesoamerican societies around the Gulf Coast Olmec centres.
materials_techniques: jade carving; ceramic incision; mirror polishing
leaves_out: 'Olmec' is an Aztec-derived name, not a self-name.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Hopewell Interaction Sphere
date_note: Middle Woodland; approximate
making_significance: Ohio and Illinois communities obtained Great Lakes copper, Appalachian mica, Gulf shells and Yellowstone obsidian to make ornaments, effigy pipes and cut-outs.
materials_techniques: copper hammering; mica cutting; pipe carving
object_types: platform pipes; copper earspools; mica cut-outs
leaves_out: 'Hopewell' is the name of a 19th-c. landowner; descendant communities are not named by it.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports
notes: Much material from mounds; NAGPRA consultation.

name: Mississippian interaction sphere
other_names: Southeastern Ceremonial Complex; Mississippian Ideological Interaction Sphere
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Mississippian towns such as Cahokia, Etowah, Moundville and Spiro shared repoussé copper plates, engraved shell gorgets and chunkey stones made from exchanged materials.
materials_techniques: copper repoussé; shell engraving; stone polishing
object_types: copper plates; shell gorgets; chunkey stones
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;play and music
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons
notes: NAGPRA consultation required.

name: Chaco road network
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Great houses in Chaco Canyon were linked by engineered roads and received turquoise, macaws and cacao from as far as Mesoamerica.
leaves_out: Descendant Pueblo communities' knowledge of the place.
free_sources: Chaco Research Archive (free; link out); UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Southwest–Mesoamerica turquoise networks
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Turquoise from mines such as Cerrillos was worked into mosaics in the Southwest; long-distance supply to Mesoamerica is now contested.
functions: clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: Recent isotope work suggests Aztec turquoise came mainly from Mesoamerican sources.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons
notes: Check Thibodeau et al. 2018 isotope study.

name: Qhapaq Ñan
date_note: Inca incorporation of earlier roads; approximate
making_significance: An Inca network of roughly 30,000 km with tambos, storehouses and fibre suspension bridges moved goods, cloth tribute and messengers across the Andes.
materials_techniques: road building; fibre suspension bridges; storage building
leaves_out: Communities rebuild the Q'eswachaka bridge annually.
free_sources: UNESCO World Heritage / Intangible Cultural Heritage pages (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Andean Spondylus trade
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Spondylus shell from warm Ecuadorian waters was traded into the Andes and worked into beads, inlays and offerings by coastal and highland makers.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; open-access excavation reports

name: Caribbean lapidary exchange (Saladoid)
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Early Ceramic Age communities of the Antilles worked and exchanged carnelian, amethyst, turquoise-like stones and Central American jadeitite into beads and frog amulets.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Fur trade
other_names: Hudson's Bay Company trade; Siberian fur trade; maritime fur trade
date_note: Russian Siberian fur tribute from 1580s; HBC from 1670
making_significance: Furs from North America and Siberia were exchanged for wool blankets, glass beads, metal and firearms, changing Indigenous clothing, beadwork and toolkits.
object_types: point blankets; beaded garments; trade silver
leaves_out: Forced tribute and coerced hunting by Indigenous peoples.
free_sources: Smithsonian NMNH Anthropology via Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 where marked); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Cape York meteorite iron use
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Inughuit and earlier Thule people worked iron from the Cape York meteorites into blades used and exchanged across the Arctic; Peary removed the meteorites in 1894–97.
leaves_out: Peary also brought six Inughuit people to New York in 1897.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons

name: Austronesian voyaging
date_note: out of Taiwan c.3000–2500 BCE; Madagascar c.500–700 CE; Aotearoa c.1250–1300
making_significance: Outrigger and double-hulled voyaging carried people, plants, pottery, barkcloth, weaving and wayfinding knowledge from Taiwan to Madagascar and Rapa Nui.
leaves_out: Present-day voyaging revival (e.g. Hōkūleʻa, 1976–).
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked; otherwise link out); Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Lapita exchange network
other_names: Lapita cultural complex; Talasea obsidian exchange
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Lapita potters made dentate-stamped vessels and moved Talasea obsidian from New Britain as far as Fiji.
functions: food and storage;exchange and value;ritual and belief
leaves_out: 'Lapita' is an archaeologists' name from a site.
free_sources: open-access excavation reports; Wikimedia Commons; Auckland Museum Online Collection (CC BY where marked)

name: Kula ring
date_note: Irwin et al. 2019 place the Ring's emergence in the last centuries before European contact (start year approximate; older estimates up to c. 1,500 years); ongoing
making_significance: Massim islanders circulate shell necklaces (soulava) and armshells (mwali) in opposite directions, with canoe building and carving tied to the exchange.
materials_techniques: shell working; canoe building; prow-board carving
defined_by: Bronisław Malinowski ('Argonauts of the Western Pacific', 1922); participants
leaves_out: Living practice; outsider accounts dominate the record.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Pitt Rivers Museum (link out)
notes: Antiquity checked against Irwin et al. 2019 (Archaeology in Oceania).

name: Hiri trade
date_note: approximate; revived as festival
making_significance: Motu women made clay pots that men sailed on lakatoi to the Gulf of Papua in exchange for sago.
leaves_out: Women potters' role.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Sepik regional exchange
date_note: antiquity undated in sources consulted; ongoing
making_significance: River and hill communities exchange pots, sago, shell valuables and carvings; Aibom women's pottery is a documented node.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles
notes: Needs expert check.

name: Maritime Jade Road
date_note: approximate (Hung et al. 2007)
making_significance: Nephrite from Fengtian in eastern Taiwan was worked into lingling-o earrings and pendants across the Philippines, Vietnam, Borneo and Thailand.
free_sources: open-access journal articles; Wikimedia Commons
notes: Taiwan coded AS-CHN;AS-ISE — check convention.

name: Dong Son bronze drum distribution
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Bronze drums cast in northern Vietnam and southern China were carried across mainland and island Southeast Asia as far as eastern Indonesia.
functions: play and music;ritual and belief;rule and display
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Macassan trepang trade
date_note: start c.1720–1780 debated; banned 1906–07
making_significance: Fleets from Makassar harvested trepang on the northern Australian coast, exchanging cloth, metal and dugout canoes with Yolŋu and other peoples.
free_sources: Trove National Library of Australia (link out; public-domain items where marked); Wikimedia Commons; open-access journal articles

name: Aboriginal exchange routes
date_note: deep antiquity; specific quarries dated variously
making_significance: Ochre, pituri, greenstone axes (e.g. Mount William quarry) and shells moved along routes across Australia, often bound to songlines.
leaves_out: Routes carry restricted knowledge.
free_sources: community-published site; Trove National Library of Australia (link out; public-domain items where marked)
notes: Community protocols apply; show only community-published material.

name: Porcelain trade
date_note: Changsha ware (Belitung wreck c.830); Jingdezhen export 14th–18th c.; Arita export from 1659; ongoing
making_significance: Chinese and later Japanese porcelain was made for export in huge quantities, copied in Persia, Delftware and Meissen, and adapted to foreign forms.
materials_techniques: underglaze cobalt; overglaze enamel; mass kiln production
functions: food and storage;exchange and value;rule and display
leaves_out: Kiln workers at Jingdezhen.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data; ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Wikimedia Commons

name: Indian cotton textile trade
date_note: cotton trade attested in the Periplus (1st c. CE); Fustat finds 10th–15th c.; European craze 1600s–1700s
making_significance: Painted and printed Indian cottons were traded from Egypt to Indonesia to Europe, prompting British calico bans (1700, 1721) and European imitation.
materials_techniques: mordant painting; block printing; resist dyeing
leaves_out: Indian dyers and painters named in few records.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Atlantic cotton economy
date_note: Whitney gin 1793 to US emancipation 1865; approximate
making_significance: Cotton grown by enslaved people in the American South fed Lancashire's mechanised mills, which then exported cheap cloth worldwide.
materials_techniques: cotton ginning; mechanised spinning and weaving
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); NYPL Digital Collections (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons

name: Sugar trade
date_note: Madeira and São Tomé 15th c.; Brazil and Caribbean 16th–19th c.
making_significance: Sugar plantations using enslaved labour drove the Atlantic economy and the European making of sugar bowls, tea services and confectionery moulds.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); NYPL Digital Collections (public-domain items); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tobacco trade
date_note: global spread from mid-16th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Tobacco from Indigenous American cultivation became a global commodity, generating pipes, snuff bottles, hookahs and tobacco boxes worldwide.
leaves_out: Indigenous ceremonial use; enslaved labour on Chesapeake plantations.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons

name: Tea trade
other_names: Canton tea trade; Kyakhta tea trade
date_note: Dutch first imports 1610; Kyakhta overland trade from 1727; Assam and Ceylon plantations 19th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Tea shaped making worldwide through teapots, cups, caddies and tea-ceremony wares, and later through plantation industries in India and Sri Lanka.
leaves_out: Indentured plantation labour in Assam and Ceylon.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); Wikimedia Commons

name: Congo Free State rubber extraction
date_note: personal rule of Leopold II 1885–1908
making_significance: Forced collection of wild rubber for bicycle and car tyres was enforced by mutilation and hostage-taking, exposed by campaigners with photographs.
leaves_out: Congolese testimony; Alice Seeley Harris's photographs.
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons; NYPL Digital Collections (public-domain items)
notes: Also Amazonian rubber boom (Putumayo) 1879–1912 — possible separate node.

name: Guano and nitrate trade
date_note: Peruvian guano boom c.1840–1880; nitrates to 1920s
making_significance: Seabird guano dug by Chinese indentured workers on the Chincha Islands fertilised European and US farms and is a case study in extraction.
leaves_out: Chinese indentured workers; War of the Pacific (1879–84).
free_sources: Library of Congress (public-domain items); Wikimedia Commons; Biodiversity Heritage Library (public domain)

name: Global container shipping
date_note: Ideal X voyage 1956; ISO container standards 1968; ongoing
making_significance: The standard steel container cut shipping costs and enabled globally dispersed manufacturing and flat-pack design.
leaves_out: Seafarers and port workers.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: The internet and platform networks
date_note: ARPANET 1969; World Wide Web 1991; platform era 2000s
making_significance: Networked computing turned design into files, templates and platforms, and made distributed and on-demand making possible.
leaves_out: Content moderators, miners of cobalt and coltan, and data-centre workers.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Sogdian merchants
date_note: Ancient Letters c.313 CE; to 8th c.
making_significance: Sogdian merchant communities in China carried silver vessels, textile designs and dance, and commissioned tombs such as that of An Jia.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons; International Dunhuang Programme (link out)

name: Armenian merchants of New Julfa
date_note: founded after Shah Abbas's deportation of Julfa Armenians 1604–05
making_significance: From Isfahan, Armenian merchant families traded silk and textiles from Amsterdam to Manila and commissioned illuminated manuscripts and churches.
leaves_out: Founding by forced deportation.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Radhanite merchants
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Jewish merchants described by Ibn Khurradadhbih (9th c.) traded brocades, furs, swords and spices between Francia and China.
leaves_out: Known almost entirely from one source.
free_sources: Internet Archive (public-domain texts); Wikimedia Commons
notes: Single-source; historians debate extent.

name: Geniza merchants
date_note: approximate
making_significance: Letters in the Cairo Geniza record Jewish merchants trading textiles, bronze, paper and dyes between the Mediterranean and India.
defined_by: S.D. Goitein; Cambridge Genizah Research Unit
free_sources: Cambridge Digital Library Taylor-Schechter Genizah (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Hadrami diaspora
date_note: earlier movements from 13th c.; main 18th–20th c.; ongoing
making_significance: Hadrami traders and scholars in Southeast Asia, East Africa and Hyderabad shaped mosque building, textile trade and remittance architecture in the Hadramawt.
leaves_out: Living communities.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Gujarati merchant communities
date_note: long-standing; documented by Tomé Pires in Melaka 1515; ongoing
making_significance: Gujarati merchants traded cloth, beads and credit around the Indian Ocean and settled in Melaka, Zanzibar and Mombasa.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Chinese maritime diaspora
other_names: Hokkien, Teochew and Cantonese diasporas; Peranakan
date_note: long-standing; ongoing
making_significance: Chinese communities in Southeast Asia and beyond created Peranakan beadwork, nyonya ware, shophouses and furniture that mixed Chinese and local making.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Met Open Access (CC0)

name: African diaspora in the Americas
date_note: ongoing
making_significance: African-descended makers created Gullah sweetgrass baskets, Afro-Brazilian metalwork, Gee's Bend quilts and the stoneware of David Drake.
functions: clothing and adornment;food and storage;ritual and belief
leaves_out: Makers whose names were not recorded.
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0); Smithsonian Open Access (CC0); Library of Congress (public-domain items); NYPL Digital Collections (public-domain items)

name: South Asian indentured diaspora
making_significance: More than a million South Asians were indentured to plantations in Mauritius, the Caribbean, Fiji and Natal, carrying textile, jewellery and building traditions.
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Huguenot craftsmen diaspora
date_note: waves from 1560s; main exodus after 1685 Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
making_significance: French Protestant refugees brought silk weaving, silversmithing and clock-making to Spitalfields, Berlin, the Dutch Republic and the Cape.
leaves_out: Persecution as cause.
free_sources: V&A collections (link out); Met Open Access (CC0); Rijksmuseum (public-domain images); Wikimedia Commons

name: Bauhaus émigrés
date_note: school closed 1933; emigration 1930s
making_significance: After the Bauhaus closed, teachers and students carried its teaching to Harvard, Black Mountain College, the New Bauhaus in Chicago, Tel Aviv and Mexico.
materials_techniques: design pedagogy; weaving; metal and furniture design
leaves_out: Bauhaus women and students who could not emigrate; some were killed in the Holocaust.
free_sources: MoMA collection (link out; metadata CC0); Harvard Art Museums (link out); Wikimedia Commons

name: Korean potters taken to Japan
other_names: forced migration of Korean potters; 'pottery wars'
date_note: Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea 1592–98
making_significance: Korean potters carried off by Japanese forces founded kilns at Arita, Satsuma, Hagi and Karatsu, starting Japanese porcelain.
object_types: Arita porcelain; Satsuma ware; Hagi tea bowls
leaves_out: Korea's losses; the potters' compulsion; Yi Sam-pyeong is credited with finding Arita porcelain stone.
free_sources: ColBase Japan national museums (Japan Government Standard Terms); National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1 where marked); Met Open Access (CC0); Wikimedia Commons
